title: Ingress-Egress Synchronization Drift — field notes
summary: Quick investigation notes on an observed tail-latency increase caused by timing drift between ingress-side flushes and egress-side buffering in proxy chains. This doc collects hypotheses, microbench setups, sample telemetry queries, and early numeric observations for follow-up experiments.
content: Context: In a recent customer-reported incident we saw spikes in 99.9th percentile token latency for streaming generation requests when routes transited an edge proxy + sidecar chain (edge -> ingress-proxy -> model-sidecar -> egress-proxy). The bulk CPU and GPU metrics looked fine. Hypothesis: subtle timing mismatch between when the upstream flushes (ingress) and when the downstream flush interval / drain window runs (egress/proxy) causes tokens to accumulate into bursts, creating micro-queueing and tail amplification in the 95–99.999 pctl. These notes capture the small-scale bench used to reproduce and some early findings.
key_findings: Tail amplification is sensitive to millisecond-scale drift between the client's flush cadence and proxy drain window offsets (observed amplification factor 1.6x–3x in 99.99p depending on config).

When ingress flush cadence and egress drain period align (phase-locked), throughput is similar but tail latency collapses. When they are anti-aligned, burst coalescence occurs at the egress buffer and triggers head-of-line delays.
Backpressure propagation is delayed by ~3–8ms in the proxy chain depending on buffer sizing and kernel scheduling, which can cause transient request-level buildup on hot paths.
Small payloads (<= 200 bytes per chunk) show a larger relative tail effect because more flush events interact with the drain window; larger payloads amortize the phase mismatch.
experiments: Bench harness: 3-node local VMs (client, edge-proxy, model-sidecar+egress-proxy cohosted). Client emits fixed-length streaming tokens at configurable flush cadence (1–20ms).
Proxy settings sweep: drain-window (5/10/20ms), max-buffer-bytes (8KB/32KB/128KB), meter-policy (immediate/periodic), scheduling niceness.
Phase sweep: systematic offset between client flush time and proxy drain boundary from 0ms to drain-window in 1ms steps. Repeat N=5000 requests per offset.
Noise injection: random sleep jitter on client (0–3ms), kernel pause on proxy (simulate scheduling), and artificial KV warmup to emulate cold-paths.
telemetry_queries: SELECT percentile(latency_ms, 99.99) FROM streaming_requests WHERE route='api.v1.generate' GROUP BY drain_phase_bin
histogram(token_ingress_ts - token_sent_ts) BY proxy_hop ORDER BY p99
trace_id WHERE span.tags contains 'egress_drain' and duration > 10ms
raw_results: Configuration: drain-window=10ms, client-cadence=4ms, buffer=32KB -> p99.99 = 48.2ms (baseline aligned) vs 127.6ms (anti-aligned).
With jitter(0-3ms): anti-aligned p99.99 distribution widened, median moved +22ms, standard deviation doubled.
Increasing buffer to 128KB reduced immediate packet drops but increased time-to-drain and worsened p99.99 by ~30% in anti-aligned tests.
interpretation_notes: This looks like a classic phase-coupling problem: periodic producers (client flushes) and periodic consumers (proxy drain windows) can create constructive interference. Larger buffers hide the problem until they become the source of longer drains. Two practical levers: (1) make drain window more continuous (smaller tick or event-driven) or (2) randomizedize ingress flush offsets (add small jitter) to de-correlate events. Also consider immediate backpressure signaling so upstream slows proactively rather than accumulating tokens.
repro_instructions: 1) Start three VMs with ubuntu-22.04 images. 2) Run edge-proxy binary with --drain-window=10ms --buffer-bytes=32768 --meter=periodic. 3) Run model-sidecar (simple echo) and cohost egress-proxy with default config. 4) Client: run bench-client --flush-ms N --tokens 1000 --trace true. 5) Sweep offset: pause client start by X ms modulo drain-window to emulate phase. 6) Collect telemetry via /metrics and traces. See attached simple bench scripts in repo linked_artifacts.
quick_patches_tested: Ingress jitter: add uniform random delay U[0,3ms] to client flush — reduced worst-case p99.99 by ~35% in anti-aligned case.
Event-driven drain: changed proxy loop to wake on socket-ready instead of periodic drain — p99.99 collapsed to near-aligned baseline but cost ~4% more CPU in steady state.
Backpressure early-signal: send synthetic RST/PAUSE upstream when buffer crosses low watermark — stabilized tails but introduced small request retries in some client HTTP stacks.
next_steps: Run same phase sweep with real model (LLM) + kv-cache enabled to see interaction with KV warmups (Diego).
Prototype adaptive drain: gradually increase drain frequency under high ingress rate and measure CPU/cost tradeoff (Aisha).
Instrument proxy to export 'drain_phase' label and add dashboard: heatmap of phase vs p99.99 by route (short term).
Add synthetic jitter to client SDKs as opt-in mitigation and run e2e customer simulation for correctness impact.
notes_to_self: Remember to test against gRPC streaming implementation too; HTTP chunking semantics and gRPC flow-control interact differently with partial frames. Also capture kernel scheduling state during worst tails (perf sched profiler) to rule out OS-level batching.
